pairs.why: Organophosphate and carbamate insecticides stop rice from breaking down propanil, so the weed killer burns the rice itself.
pairs.fix: Keep at least 14 days between {a} and {b}, before or after. Choose an insecticide from another group if you must spray sooner.

pairs.why: The bispyribac label warns that propanil and malathion weaken it or injure the rice.
pairs.fix: Keep about 7 days between {a} and {b}.

pairs.why: The bispyribac label bans crop oil with it.
pairs.fix: Use the spreader its label names instead of an oil.

pairs.why: Corn cannot break down these sulfonylurea weed killers while an organophosphate insecticide is in it, and the corn is stunted or burned.
pairs.fix: Do not spray {a} with {b}. Keep about 7 days between them, and check the label if an organophosphate went into the soil at planting.

pairs.why: Bentazon with nicosulfuron can badly injure corn, and 2,4-D in the same tank weakens its grass control.
pairs.fix: Spray {a} on its own day.

pairs.why: The cyhalofop rice label bans these partners because grass control drops.
pairs.fix: Spray {a} on the grasses first and {b} about a week later.

pairs.why: Broadleaf weed killers often weaken grass killers like {a} when they share a tank, so the grasses may survive.
pairs.fix: Spray {a} on the grasses first and {b} some days apart, or use a product sold with both on one label.

pairs.why: The cyhalofop rice label names {b} as a partner.
The fenoxaprop rice label names {b} as a partner.
Propanil and {b} are sold together on labels here.
The bispyribac rice label names {b} as a partner.
Two weed killers in one tank can each work less, or together burn the crop, unless a label names the mix.
pairs.fix: Mix them only if one of the labels names the other. Jar test first.

pairs.why: A fast burning weed killer can kill the leaves before glyphosate travels to the roots, so tough and perennial weeds may grow back.
pairs.fix: For grasses with deep roots, spray glyphosate alone and wait about a week before a burndown.

pairs.why: Atrazine can make glyphosate work less when they are mixed.
pairs.fix: Spray glyphosate first to clear the weeds, then atrazine.

pairs.why: Oil helps atrazine on weeds that are up, but in some weather it can burn the corn.
pairs.fix: Use the oil only as the atrazine label says, and not on stressed corn.

pairs.why: Calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc and other minerals bind glyphosate in the tank, and it kills fewer weeds.
pairs.fix: Never add a foliar fertilizer to glyphosate. The only fertilizer that helps it is spray grade ammonium sulfate, added to the water first.

pairs.why: Metals in foliar fertilizer bind weak acid weed killers like {a}, and they work less.
pairs.fix: Spray the weed killer without the fertilizer.

pairs.why: Ammonium sulfate ties up hard water minerals before they reach the weed killer, a mix the labels allow.
pairs.fix: Dissolve the ammonium sulfate in the water before you add {a}.

pairs.why: The amine salt of 2,4-D mixes well with nitrogen fertilizer only; with NPK solutions it may not stay mixed.
pairs.fix: Jar test first, or spray them on different days.

pairs.why: Fertilizer in the tank raises crop injury from {a}.
pairs.fix: Spray the weed killer in water only, and the fertilizer on another day.

pairs.why: Fertilizer in the tank can make a weed killer burn the crop, and the salt can keep products from mixing.
pairs.fix: Mix fertilizer with {a} only if its label allows it. Otherwise spray them on different days.

pairs.why: {a} kills or hurts any green plant it touches, so a tank mixed for the crop will hurt the crop.
pairs.fix: Use {a} only on weeds before planting, between rows with a shield, or where its label allows. Spray crop products in their own tank.

pairs.why: Oil and sulfur together, or close together, burn leaves and fruit.
pairs.fix: Keep at least two weeks between an oil spray and a sulfur spray.

pairs.why: Lime sulfur soon after an oil burns the leaves.
pairs.fix: Keep a month between an oil spray and lime sulfur.

pairs.why: Captan and folpet with an oil, or sprayed close to one, burn the crop.
pairs.fix: Spray {b} alone, days away from any oil spray.

pairs.why: Chlorothalonil with an oil can injure the plants.
pairs.fix: Spray them on different days.

pairs.why: The oil labels ban carbaryl and dimethoate in the mix.
pairs.fix: Spray them on different days.

pairs.why: Spray oil labels ban NPK foliar fertilizer in the mix.
pairs.fix: Spray the foliar fertilizer on its own day.

pairs.why: The captan label bans organophosphate EC products, with their solvents, in the mix.
pairs.fix: Use another formulation of the insecticide, or spray them apart.

pairs.why: Two strong spreaders together wet the leaf so much that the spray can burn it and runs off.
pairs.fix: Use one spreader only, the one the main product label names.

pairs.why: Strobilurin fungicides like {a} mixed with an EC product, an oil or a silicone spreader have burned some crops, more so in cool cloudy weather.
pairs.fix: Jar test, then spray a few plants and look again after three to seven days before you spray the field.

pairs.why: Insecticidal soap with sulfur can injure plants.
pairs.fix: Keep three days between them.

pairs.why: Insecticidal soap does not stay mixed with calcium, foliar fertilizers, chelates, fosetyl or acids, and may burn the crop.
pairs.fix: Spray the soap alone in soft water.

pairs.why: The soap label says it mixes with Bt and spinosad.
Lime sulfur is strongly alkaline and reacts with most products, breaking them down, burning the crop, or with acids and phosphates giving off a toxic gas.
pairs.fix: Spray lime sulfur alone, and keep a week or two before and after other sprays, a month from any oil.

pairs.why: Bordeaux mixture carries lime, and its high pH breaks down {b} in the tank.
pairs.fix: Spray Bordeaux alone. Choose a copper without lime if you need copper with {b}.

pairs.why: {a} makes the water strongly alkaline, and {b} breaks down quickly in alkaline water, so the spray loses its strength in the tank.
pairs.fix: Spray them on different days, or spray {b} in water that is neutral or slightly acid.

pairs.why: {a} raises the pH of the tank, and {b} slowly loses strength in alkaline water.
pairs.fix: If you mix them, spray at once and never leave the tank standing.

pairs.why: The thiophanate methyl label bans copper in the tank.
pairs.fix: Spray them on different days.

pairs.why: Potassium bicarbonate makes the spray mildly alkaline: acids weaken it, and it breaks down products that do not like alkaline water.
pairs.fix: Spray it alone.

pairs.why: Ethephon must stay acid. In alkaline water it turns into ethylene gas in the tank and is lost.
pairs.fix: Spray ethephon alone in clean water, at once after mixing.

pairs.why: Glyphosate products already carry what they need; the labels say not to add buffers or acidifiers when it is sprayed alone.
pairs.fix: Leave the acidifier out. For hard water use spray grade ammonium sulfate.

pairs.why: Fosetyl aluminium is acid and frees copper into a form that burns leaves and fruit.
pairs.fix: Spray copper and fosetyl on different days.

pairs.why: Acid phosphite sprays on copper, or copper on fresh phosphite, can burn the leaves.
pairs.fix: Keep about three weeks between them, or raise the phosphite spray to pH 6 or more as its label says.

pairs.why: Acid spray water dissolves copper into free ions that burn the leaves.
pairs.fix: Never lower the pH of a copper spray. Keep it at pH 6.5 or more.

pairs.why: Copper with mancozeb is a common mix against blights and leaf spots; the labels list it and premixes are sold.
pairs.fix: Premix each powder in a little water before it goes into the tank.

pairs.why: The sulfur label lists copper fungicides as compatible.
Foliar fertilizer with {a} has burned some crops.
pairs.fix: Spray the fertilizer on another day, or test a few plants first.

pairs.why: {a} kills fungi, and {b} is a living fungus.
pairs.fix: Spray {b} alone, and keep a few days between it and any fungicide, as its label says.

pairs.why: {b} harms the living Trichoderma in {a}.
pairs.fix: Keep about a week between them.

pairs.why: {a} can kill the living organisms in {b}.
pairs.fix: Spray the living product alone, in clean water, a few days apart from {a}.

pairs.why: One chlorothalonil label bans mixing with Bt because some plants were injured.
pairs.fix: Spray them on different days.

pairs.why: Two living products can compete in the tank.
pairs.fix: Mix them only if one of the labels says they go together.

pairs.why: Peroxides and chlorine products react with other products and break them down. They are not for a crop tank mix.
pairs.fix: Use {a} alone, only as its label says.

pairs.why: Calcium with phosphate, and strong calcium with sulfates, can settle out as a solid in the tank.
pairs.fix: Jar test at the real strength. Better, spray the calcium on its own day, or use a chelated calcium.

pairs.why: Potassium silicate turns into a gel or a white sludge with calcium, magnesium and metal salts.
pairs.fix: Spray potassium silicate alone, in its own tank.

pairs.why: Potassium silicate is strongly alkaline (pH 11 to 12) and reacts with acids and acid fertilizers, setting into a gel.
pairs.fix: Spray potassium silicate alone. Add it to the water first, then nothing else.

pairs.why: Phosphate locks zinc, iron, manganese, copper and magnesium salts into solids that settle out and clog the nozzle.
pairs.fix: Use chelated micronutrients with a phosphate fertilizer, or spray them on different days.

pairs.why: Boron and calcium can settle out together when strong, and boron burns crops at rates only a little above need.
pairs.fix: Jar test at the real strength, or use a calcium and boron product made to go together.

pairs.why: Thiosulfate breaks down in acid, dropping sulfur and gas, and settles out with calcium.
pairs.fix: Keep thiosulfate fertilizers away from acids and calcium.

pairs.why: Humic and fulvic products clump in acid water and with calcium and metal salts.
pairs.fix: Jar test first. Spray the humic product alone if it clumps.

pairs.why: Phosphite and calcium can settle out as a solid when strong.
pairs.fix: Jar test first, or spray them apart.

pairs.why: Urea mixed with ammonium nitrate or calcium nitrate pulls water from the air and turns into a wet paste.
pairs.fix: Spread them separately, or spread one right after the other without mixing them in the bag.

pairs.why: Urea and superphosphate (solophos, triple superphosphate) react and get wet and lumpy when they sit mixed.
pairs.fix: Mix them only just before you spread, and spread the same hour.

pairs.why: Lime and other alkaline materials turn the nitrogen of urea and ammonium fertilizers into ammonia gas that is lost to the air.
pairs.fix: Spread the lime first and work it in, then wait about two weeks before urea or ammonium fertilizers. If you must, work the nitrogen into the soil or water it in at once.

pairs.why: Lime mixed with phosphate fertilizer turns part of the phosphorus into a form the roots take up slowly.
pairs.fix: Spread the lime first and the phosphate later, or place the phosphate in a band.

pairs.why: Calcium nitrate with water soluble phosphates turns the phosphate into a form roots take up poorly, and the blend goes wet.
pairs.fix: Spread them separately.

pairs.why: Calcium nitrate pulls water from the air very fast, so a blend with it goes wet and sticky.
pairs.fix: Spread calcium nitrate on its own, or mix only what you spread in the next few minutes.

pairs.why: Mixing a pesticide into fertilizer by hand spreads it unevenly and puts the person mixing it at risk.
pairs.fix: Apply the pesticide granules as their label says, or buy a fertilizer that already carries them.

pairs.why: Fresh lime is harsh on the living microbes of a biofertilizer.
pairs.fix: Spread the biofertilizer a week or two after the lime.

hard_glyphosate.why: Hard water (deep wells, water that leaves a white crust) weakens {a}.
hard_glyphosate.fix: Dissolve spray grade ammonium sulfate in the water first, as the label of the weed killer or the ammonium sulfate says, then add the weed killer. Or use rain water.

muddy_binders.why: Clay in muddy water binds {a} and takes it out of the spray.
muddy_binders.fix: Use clear water from a well or a clean drum, never canal or river water that is brown.

alk_water.why: {a} breaks down in alkaline water, and well water here is often alkaline.
alk_water.fix: Spray within an hour or two of mixing and never leave the tank overnight. A spray buffer helps, unless the tank has copper or a sulfonylurea weed killer.

ph_conflict.why: {a} last longer in slightly acid water, but {b} break down in acid water.
ph_conflict.fix: Do not add an acidifier. Keep the water near neutral, pH 6.5 to 7, and spray at once.

too_many.why: Four or more products in one tank raise the chance that something settles, fails or burns.
too_many.fix: Jar test the whole mix first. Leave out what is not needed this time.

same_ai.why: {a} and {b} carry the same active ingredient, {ai}. Two doses in one tank is double the dose.

same_group.why: {a} and {b} work the same way ({grp}). Two of one group adds little, and the pest learns to survive it sooner.
same_group.fix: Keep one, and pair it with a product from another group.

salt_emulsion.why: Strong fertilizer in the tank can break the milky emulsion of EC products or clump powders.
salt_emulsion.fix: Add the fertilizer last and stir well, or spray the fertilizer on its own day.

bait_in_tank.why: {a} is a bait or granule that goes on as it is. It is not mixed in water.
bait_in_tank.fix: Put it out as its label says, on its own.

seed_in_tank.why: {a} is a seed treatment. It goes on the seed before planting, not in a field spray.
seed_in_tank.fix: Treat the seed with it as its label says.

heat_sulfur.why: Sulfur burns leaves and fruit when it is hotter than about 32 C, now or in the next days. Spreaders make it worse.
heat_sulfur.fix: Spray sulfur early in the morning on a cool day, or choose another fungicide in hot weather.

heat_oil.why: Spray oils burn leaves in the heat, in very humid air and on plants short of water.
heat_oil.fix: Spray oil in the cool of the early morning or late in the day, on watered plants, below about 32 C.

heat_fert.why: Foliar fertilizer dries fast in the heat and the salt left on the leaf burns it.
heat_fert.fix: Spray in the cool of the early morning or late in the day, and keep the strength at the lower end.

rain_soon.why: Rain soon after spraying washes contact products and foliar fertilizer off the leaves.
rain_soon.fix: Spray when no rain is expected for a few hours. A sticker helps contact products stay on.

copper_young_cucurbit.why: {crop} and all young, tender growth burn easily with copper, more so when the leaves stay wet.
copper_young_cucurbit.fix: Use the lowest label rate on young plants, spray in dry weather, and test on a few plants first.

sulfur_cucurbit.why: Sulfur can injure melons, cucumbers, squash and gourds, more so in heat.
sulfur_cucurbit.fix: Test on a few plants first, or choose another fungicide.

heat_propanil.why: Propanil labels ban spraying when it is hotter than 32 C.
heat_propanil.fix: Spray {a} in the cool of the early morning or late in the day, on a cooler day.

heat_limesulfur.why: Lime sulfur burns the leaves when it is hotter than about 29 C.
heat_limesulfur.fix: Spray it on a cool morning, or choose another product in the hot season.

not_labelled.why: The label of {a} does not name {crop}.
not_labelled.fix: Use a product labelled for your crop, or check with your agriculture technician first.

herb_crop_not_labelled.why: The label of {a} does not name {crop}. A weed killer not made for your crop can kill it.
herb_crop_not_labelled.fix: Choose a weed killer labelled for {crop}.

fpa_restricted.fix: Use it only as the FPA allows.

strength_fert.why: The fertilizer in this spray comes to {pct} percent ({gl} grams in a liter). For {crop} {stage}, keep it under {lim} percent or the leaves can burn.
strength_fert.fix: Use more water or less fertilizer: about {max} in the tank you set.

strength_urea.why: Urea in this spray comes to {pct} percent. For {crop} {stage}, keep urea under {lim} percent.
strength_urea.fix: Use about {max} of urea in the tank you set.

salt_seedling.why: High salt fertilizers ({a}) burn young roots when they lie close to them.
salt_seedling.fix: Keep it a hand width away from the seedlings and water it in. Split the dose into two applications.

ph_high.why: Your water is pH {ph}, alkaline, and {a} breaks down in alkaline water.
ph_high.fix: Spray within an hour of mixing. A spray buffer brings the water to about pH 6, unless the tank has copper, a sulfonylurea or soap.

ph_low_copper.why: Your water is pH {ph}. Copper in acid water turns into free ions that burn leaves.
ph_low_copper.fix: Spray {a} in water at pH 6.5 or more, and never add an acidifier to it.

ph_low_su.why: Your water is pH {ph}, and {a} breaks down faster in acid water.
ph_low_su.fix: Do not add an acidifier. Spray it at once after mixing.

salt_seed.why: About {nk} kg of nitrogen and potash per hectare would sit right with the seed or young roots. More than about 11 kg there can burn them.
salt_seed.fix: Keep most of it a hand width away from the seed or the row, or split it: a little at planting and the rest later as top dress.

urea_dry_surface.why: Urea and ammonium left on dry soil turn into ammonia gas, and much of the nitrogen is lost to the air.
urea_dry_surface.fix: Spread them on moist soil just before rain or irrigation, water them in within a day or two, or work them into the soil.

nitrate_flooded.why: Nitrate fertilizer in flooded soil is soon lost as gas or washed down, before the roots take it up.
nitrate_flooded.fix: In a flooded field use urea or ammonium fertilizers, and keep nitrate for upland crops or drained soil.

urea_wet_leaves.why: Granules that stay on wet leaves burn spots in them.
urea_wet_leaves.fix: Spread when the leaves are dry and shake or wash the granules off the plants.

not_spray.why: {a} is made to spread on the soil, not to spray. Granules dissolve slowly, and the filler in them settles and clogs the nozzle.
not_spray.fix: Use a soluble or foliar grade instead, or leave it out of the tank and spread it.

not_spray_pest.why: {a} is a granule pesticide, made to spread as it is. Its label does not tell you to mix it in water.
not_spray_pest.fix: Spread it on its own as its label says, and leave it out of the tank.

not_granule.why: {a} goes on in water, by spray or drench. Spread dry with granules, it does not reach where it works.
not_granule.fix: Leave it out of the blend and spray it on its own trip, or choose A spray above to check it with your other sprays.

bait_in_blend.why: {a} is a bait that goes on as it is. It is not blended with fertilizer.
bait_in_blend.fix: Put it out as its label says, on its own.

seed_in_blend.why: {a} is a seed treatment. It goes on the seed before planting, not in a fertilizer blend.
seed_in_blend.fix: Treat the seed with it as its label says.

order.say: Start with a clean sprayer and clear water. Fill it about half way and keep it moving: shake or stir as you add each product, one at a time.
Add the water conditioner first ({items}) and let it dissolve fully.
Add the powders and granules ({items}), one at a time. Premix each in a small pail of water into a smooth milk first, then pour it in.
Shake or stir well until the powder is spread through the water.
Add the water based liquids ({items}). Shake each bottle first.
Add the solutions and soluble powders ({items}).
Add the oil based liquids ({items}). The water turns milky.
Add the spreader, sticker or oil ({items}).
Add the foliar fertilizer last ({items}). Dissolve powders in a pail of water first.
Top up with water to the mark, keep mixing, and spray at once. Never leave the mix standing or overnight.

jar: Use a clean, clear glass jar or bottle with a lid, only for this. Wear the gloves the labels ask for.
Pour in half a liter of the same water you will spray, from the same source.
Add each product in the tank order, at the amounts below (the tank rate for one liter), closing and turning the jar over about 10 times after each.
Top up to one liter, mix again, and let it stand at least 15 minutes, 30 is safer.
Look for layers, oil on top, flakes or lumps, sludge or gel, heavy foam, heat or a strong smell. If it stays even, or comes back with a gentle shake, it mixes.
If it fails, spray the products separately. A jar test cannot show burn or loss of strength: spray a few plants first and look again after three to seven days.

all: Weigh each fertilizer for the area you will cover, then mix them on a dry tarp or floor in the shade, only what you spread today.
Wear gloves and keep the dust off your face. Close the bags right away: blends take up water from the air.
broadcast: Spread evenly by hand or with a spreader, half going one way across the field and half the other way, so no spot gets a double dose.
incorporated: Spread it evenly, then work it into the top few centimeters of soil the same day with a rake, a harrow or the last plowing.
band: Put it in a shallow furrow a hand width beside the row, then cover it with soil.
hole: Put it in the bottom of the hole, cover it with a little soil, then plant on top, so the seed or roots do not touch the fertilizer.
spread.pesticide: Apply the pesticide granules as their label says. Mix them into fertilizer only if both labels allow it, wearing gloves.
after: Water it in, or let the rain or the irrigation carry it into the soil. In a paddy, keep the water in for a few days after.
